Islamic Festivals: Celebration and Commemoration

Islamic festivals mark pivotal moments in the history of Islam and the lives of the prophets. They serve both to celebrate Allah’s blessings and to deepen a Muslim’s understanding of their faith. Some festivals are observed by all Muslims; others are particular to Shi’a practice. The calendar is lunar, so festival dates move earlier each year relative to the Western calendar.

Eid-ul-Adha: The Festival of Sacrifice

Eid-ul-Adha is one of the two major festivals celebrated by all Muslims, both Sunni and Shi’a. It falls on the 10th of Dhul Hijjah, at the end of the Hajj pilgrimage. The festival commemorates the story of the Prophet Ibrahim, who was commanded by Allah to sacrifice his son Isma’il. Just as Ibrahim was about to obey, Allah intervened and provided a ram to sacrifice in Isma’il’s place — a sign of divine mercy and a reward for absolute obedience.

Muslims worldwide mark Eid-ul-Adha by performing a communal prayer in the mosque or an open space, followed by the sacrifice (qurbani) of an animal — typically a sheep, goat, cow or camel. The meat is divided into three portions: one third for the family, one third for friends and neighbours, and one third given to those in need. This act of sharing reflects the Islamic values of generosity, gratitude and care for the community. For Muslims not on Hajj, it is still a major celebration of Ibrahim’s faith.

Eid-ul-Fitr: Ending the Fast

Eid-ul-Fitr is celebrated on the first day of the month of Shawwal, immediately after Ramadan. It is a joyful occasion that marks the successful completion of a month of fasting, prayer and reflection. Muslims begin the day with a communal prayer, wear new or best clothes, give gifts — especially to children — and share meals with family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims are required to pay Zakat al-Fitr, a special form of charitable giving to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can share in the celebration. Eid-ul-Fitr lasts for one day (though in some cultures celebrations continue over several days).

Key Fact

Eid-ul-Adha (end of Hajj) commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice Isma’il; animal sacrifice and sharing of meat are central. Eid-ul-Fitr (end of Ramadan) celebrates the completion of fasting; communal prayer, Zakat al-Fitr and family celebration are key features. Both are observed by Sunni and Shi’a Muslims worldwide.

Eid-ul-Ghadeer and Ashura: Shi’a Festivals

Two further festivals are observed primarily by Shi’a Muslims. Eid-ul-Ghadeer is celebrated on 18 Dhul Hijjah, three days after Eid-ul-Adha. It commemorates the event at the pool of Ghadir Khumm, where Shi’a Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad publicly designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali as his rightful successor and leader of the Muslim community (the Imam). Sunni Muslims do not observe this festival, as they do not share the Shi’a belief about Ali’s designated leadership.

Ashura is observed on the 10th of Muharram (the first month of the Islamic calendar) and is the most solemn Shi’a commemoration. It marks the martyrdom of Hussayn ibn Ali, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the third Shi’a Imam, who was killed along with his family and companions at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Hussayn refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims regard as illegitimate. His death is seen as an act of principled martyrdom in defence of justice and Islam.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most important date of the year — a day of intense mourning, public processions, lamentation poetry (marthiya), communal prayers, and plays re-enacting the events at Karbala (ta’ziyeh). Many Shi’a communities in Iraq, Iran and beyond hold large-scale commemorations. For Sunni Muslims, Ashura has a different significance — it marks the day Moses and the Israelites were saved from Pharaoh, and many Sunni Muslims observe an optional fast on this day, following the practice of the Prophet Muhammad. This contrast — grief and lamentation for Shi’a, a quieter fast for Sunni — illustrates how the same date can carry very different meanings across the Muslim world.

Jihad: Greater and Lesser

The word Jihad means ‘striving’ or ‘struggle’ in the way of Allah. It is widely misunderstood — it does not simply mean ‘holy war’. Islamic tradition divides Jihad into two distinct categories: Greater (al-jihad al-akbar) and Lesser (al-jihad al-asghar).

The Greater Jihad is the inner, personal struggle against one’s own ego, desires, selfishness, anger and moral failings — striving to live according to “the straight path” (as-sirat al-mustaqim). This is considered the more difficult and more important form of Jihad. A widely-cited saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad after a military campaign describes him as saying they had returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle — the struggle against the self. Though its chain of transmission is disputed by many hadith scholars (classical authorities including Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani and al-Albani classify it as weak), the theological concept it expresses has shaped Islamic spiritual understanding across the centuries. The concepts of Ma’ruf (what is right and good) and Munkar (what is wrong and evil) are central to Greater Jihad: striving for the straight path means actively promoting Ma’ruf and resisting Munkar in oneself and society.

Key Fact

Greater Jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) is the spiritual struggle against the lower self (nafs) — the most important form. Lesser Jihad (al-jihad al-asghar) is the outward, defensive struggle. Islamic tradition is explicit that Greater Jihad takes precedence over Lesser Jihad.

Lesser Jihad and Its Conditions

The Lesser Jihad refers to outward struggle, which in classical Islamic jurisprudence is strictly defensive — it may be waged only when the Muslim community is under attack, when innocent people are being oppressed, or when evil cannot be removed by other means. The Qur’an sets boundaries: “Fight in the cause of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress limits; for Allah loves not transgressors” (Surah 2:190, al-Baqarah). The Qur’an also commands that if an enemy seeks peace, Muslims must accept it: “But if they incline to peace, then incline to it also and put your trust in Allah” (Surah 8:61, al-Anfal).

The mainstream Islamic scholarly tradition (including bodies such as Al-Azhar University) holds that armed Jihad is only ever defensive and subject to strict conditions: it must be declared by legitimate authority, it must be the last resort, civilians and non-combatants must be protected, and it must cease when the enemy seeks peace. A minority of extremist groups have argued that offensive Jihad is justified to spread Islam — a view that is rejected by the vast majority of Muslim scholars and communities worldwide as a distortion of Islamic teaching. Examiners expect students to present both the mainstream position and divergent views, without endorsing any form of political violence.

What Is God Like?

One of the biggest questions in philosophy and religion is: what is God actually like? Religious traditions answer this question in rich and varied ways. Most Christians understand God through three key qualities: God is omnipotent, knowing everything past, present and future (omniscient), and perfectly good. These qualities are called the “divine attributes.” For many believers, understanding God’s nature is essential — it shapes how they pray, how they act, and how they make sense of suffering.

Christians believe God is deeply personal: a being who created the universe not out of necessity but out of love, and who continues to be involved in the lives of people. The letter of 1 John 4:8 makes this claim directly: “God is love.” This short statement carries enormous weight. It suggests that love is not just something God does — it is what God fundamentally is. This framing shapes how Christians respond to suffering and evil.

Key Fact

The three core divine attributes are omnipotence (all-powerful), omniscience (all-knowing) and omnibenevolence (all-loving or all-good). Together they form the classical theistic view of God and provide the basis for the problem of evil.

God’s Relationship With the World

Believers also debate how God relates to the world he created. A transcendent God is utterly beyond the universe — distant, wholly other, not directly involved in day-to-day events. By contrast, an immanent God is close and personally active, felt in everyday life. Most mainstream Christian traditions hold both: God is transcendent in greatness and yet immanent through the Holy Spirit, prayer, and the life of Jesus Christ.

The parable of the Prodigal Son in Luke 15:11–32 captures this sense of an immanent, personally involved God. The father in the story runs to meet his returning son — a picture of God actively pursuing a relationship with humanity rather than remaining remote. For believers, this parable shows that God’s relationship with the world is not passive but active and loving.

God as Good: What Does Goodness Mean?

Religious believers argue that God is the source and standard of all goodness. Genesis 1:31 records that after God finished creation, “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good.” This suggests that goodness is built into the fabric of creation. God does not merely follow a moral code that exists independently — God is the moral order. When believers say God is good, they mean his actions, character and purposes are never destructive or selfish.

However, believers disagree about what divine goodness means in practice. Some argue that God’s goodness is the same as human moral goodness, only perfect. Others say God’s goodness is so far beyond human understanding that we can only speak of it by analogy. The medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas argued we use language about God “analogically” — terms like “good” apply to God in a related but not identical way to how they apply to people.

Many Christians believe God’s goodness is expressed through his benevolence — his care and mercy towards all humanity. They point to passages like Psalm 23 (“The Lord is my shepherd”) and the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus calls his followers to reflect God’s goodness through love, compassion and justice.

Some denominations, particularly within the Reformed tradition, emphasise God’s justice alongside his love — arguing that goodness also means God cannot ignore wrongdoing. Evangelical Christians often stress that God’s goodness is shown supremely in the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, who took on human sin so that people could be forgiven and restored to relationship with God.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

The most challenging objection to belief in God is the problem of evil. The argument runs like this: if God is omnipotent, he could prevent suffering. If he is omnibenevolent, he would want to prevent it. Yet suffering clearly exists. So either God is not all-powerful, or not all-good — or does not exist at all. This is what philosophers call the “logical problem of evil.”

Suffering takes two forms. Moral evil arises from human choices — such as violence, theft or oppression. Natural evil arises from the natural world — earthquakes, cancer, floods. Non-believers often argue that natural evil is especially difficult to explain, since it cannot be blamed on human free will.

Key Fact

Moral evil and natural evil together form the “problem of evil.” The dilemma is ancient: it was expressed in Psalm 22:1 when the psalmist cries, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” — and in the Book of Job, where a righteous man suffers without apparent cause.

Religious Responses to Suffering

Religious believers have developed a range of responses to this challenge. One of the most important is the “free will defence.” God gave humans free will — the genuine ability to choose good or evil. Without this freedom, human beings would be moral robots, incapable of love or virtue. Moral evil is therefore a consequence of human freedom, not evidence against God’s goodness.

A second response concerns the purpose of suffering. The prophet Jeremiah, speaking on God’s behalf in Jeremiah 5:19, frames suffering as a consequence of turning away from God — a call to return. This does not mean God causes every individual suffering as punishment, but that suffering can prompt repentance, growth and a deeper relationship with God.

Many believers also point to the example of Jesus Christ, who suffered on the cross. Far from being absent from suffering, in the Christian tradition God entered into it. This is called the “theology of the cross” or divine solidarity. For many Christians, the resurrection then shows that suffering does not have the final word.

Atheists and agnostics argue that the existence of widespread, apparently pointless suffering is strong evidence against an all-powerful, all-good God. The philosopher J.L. Mackie argued that the co-existence of God and evil is a logical contradiction — a truly omnipotent God could create free beings who always freely chose good.

Humanists respond to suffering by emphasising human responsibility: rather than praying for divine intervention, the moral response is human action — working to reduce poverty, disease and injustice. Many non-believers also argue that natural disasters show a universe that is indifferent to human welfare, not one designed by a loving creator. In a 15-mark “Discuss” response, presenting these views fairly alongside religious responses demonstrates the evaluative thinking examiners reward.

The Islamic tradition also engages with this question. Muslims affirm that Allah is Ar-Rahman (the Most Gracious) and Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful), and that trials and suffering are a test of faith and a means of spiritual purification, not evidence of divine absence. This perspective reflects the multi-faith nature of the theme as examined on this paper.

The Purpose and Forms of Christian Worship

Worship is at the heart of Christian life. Christians worship to thank God, to ask for forgiveness, to seek guidance and to strengthen their relationship with him. The New Testament describes God as spirit, and Christians are called to worship “in spirit and in truth” (John 4:24). This means true worship comes from the heart, not just outward ritual.

Worship takes many forms. The key distinction is between liturgical worship — which follows a set structure — and informal or charismatic worship, which is free-flowing. Both forms are used across different Christian denominations.

Liturgical Worship

Liturgical worship is led by an ordained minister who guides the congregation through a fixed order: readings, prayers, a sermon and symbolic actions. The Anglican Communion service and the Roman Catholic mass are the most widely practised forms of liturgical worship. The Greek Orthodox service is similarly structured but draws deeply on ancient Eastern traditions, including elaborate chanting and the use of incense and icons.

Supporters of liturgical worship value its continuity with centuries of Christian tradition. It provides a sense of unity — Roman Catholics or Orthodox Christians can follow the same Mass structure anywhere in the world. The set readings ensure the whole Bible is covered over time, and the formal prayers focus the mind on God rather than personal preference.

Methodist Sunday morning worship has a flexible order — it may include hymns, prayers, a Bible reading, a sermon and a collection — but the exact shape changes each week. It is informal enough to respond to the congregation’s needs while still structured enough to be recognisable as a church service.

A Quaker meeting is radically different. There is no ordained leader, no set prayers and no music. Worshippers sit in silent waiting until someone feels moved by the Spirit to speak. This practice is rooted in the belief that God can speak directly to every individual. Some Quaker meetings pass in almost total silence.

Key Fact

The specification names five worship traditions: Anglican Communion service (liturgical), Roman Catholic mass (liturgical), Greek Orthodox service (liturgical), Methodist Sunday morning worship (informal) and Quaker meeting (silent, Spirit-led). Examiners expect you to know at least two of these with their key features.

The Role of the Holy Spirit in Worship

The New Testament teaches that Christians are led by the Spirit of God (Romans 8:14). For charismatic Christians, this means worship can include speaking in tongues, prophetic words and physical expressions of joy such as raised hands or dance. Pentecostal churches in particular emphasise the gifts of the Spirit. Others, like the Quakers, seek the Spirit through silent waiting. In both cases, worship is seen as more than outward action — it is an encounter with the living God.

The Sacraments

A sacrament is an outward sign of an inward grace — a physical action that communicates God’s love and forgiveness. Roman Catholics recognise seven sacraments (including baptism, Eucharist, confession, confirmation, marriage, holy orders and anointing of the sick). Most Protestant denominations recognise only two: Baptism and the Eucharist. Quakers and members of the Salvation Army reject sacramental practices entirely, arguing that all of life can be an act of worship.

Matthew 3:13–17 describes the baptism of Jesus by John in the River Jordan. As Jesus came out of the water, the Spirit descended on him like a dove — linking baptism with the Holy Spirit. Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox Christians practise infant baptism: parents and godparents make promises on behalf of the child, who is baptised with water. This is seen as welcoming the child into the covenant community of the Church.

Baptists and many evangelical Christians practise believers’ baptism (also called adult or full-immersion baptism). They argue that baptism should follow a personal confession of faith, as seen in the Great Commission (Matthew 28). The candidate is fully immersed in water, symbolising death to the old self and resurrection to new life in Christ. Baptists argue infant baptism has no biblical basis since infants cannot make a personal commitment.

Key Fact

At the Last Supper, Jesus said: “This is my body” and “This is my blood of the covenant” (Matthew 26:26–28). Paul also records this in 1 Corinthians 11:23–26, adding “do this in remembrance of me.” These texts are the scriptural foundation for the Eucharist and are cited differently by different denominations to support transubstantiation, consubstantiation, or a purely memorial view.

The Eucharist: Shared Ritual, Disputed Meaning

The Eucharist (also called Holy Communion, the Mass or the Lord’s Supper) is the most contested sacrament among Christians. Roman Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ while their outward appearance remains unchanged. Lutherans hold consubstantiation: Christ is truly present in, with and under the elements. Most Protestant denominations, including Methodists and Baptists, view the Eucharist as a memorial — a symbolic act of remembrance, not a physical transformation. 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 is the key scriptural anchor for all views.

Prayer: Individual and Communal

Prayer is communication with God. It can be spoken or silent, individual or corporate. Christians believe God listens and responds to prayer. The New Testament teaches that where two or three gather in Jesus’s name, he is present with them (Matthew 18:20), showing that communal prayer has a special significance. Equally, Jesus encouraged private prayer as a personal encounter with God.

The types of prayer recognised in Christian tradition include: adoration, confession, thanksgiving, intercessions and supplication. Charismatic Christians also practise ‘praying in the spirit’ (glossolalia), chants and meditational prayers. Paul describes how the Spirit helps believers pray when they do not know what to say (Romans 8:26), and 1 Corinthians 14:26–40 gives practical guidance on orderly use of spiritual gifts in communal worship.

The Lord’s Prayer

When the disciples asked Jesus how to pray, he gave them a model. Luke’s version appears in Luke 11:1–4; Matthew’s fuller version, including the doxology (“for thine is the kingdom”) familiar from church use, is in Matthew 6:9–13 (the preceding verses, 6:5–8, contain Jesus’s instruction not to pray ostentatiously). The Lord’s Prayer combines praise (“hallowed be your name”), submission to God’s will, a request for daily provision, forgiveness and protection from evil. Jesus also warned against ostentatious public prayer, saying true prayer should be private and sincere rather than performed to impress others.

The Lord’s Prayer is used in both public liturgical worship and private devotion. It unites Christians of all denominations — from Roman Catholic Mass to the simplest Protestant home prayer. Its use of “Our Father” reminds believers that prayer is not just individual but a communal relationship with God as parent of all.

Liturgical traditions (Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox) favour extempore prayer alongside set prayers from authorised books such as the Book of Common Prayer or the Roman Missal. These provide theological precision and prevent heresy creeping into public worship.

Many evangelical and charismatic Christians prefer entirely spontaneous, extempore prayer, arguing that set prayers can become mechanical and lose their sincerity. They point to Romans 8:14 as evidence that the Spirit should guide the words of prayer in the moment. In practice, most Christians use both types at different times — corporate set prayers in church and personal spontaneous prayer at home.

Islam as a Way of Life

Islam is not simply a set of beliefs — it is a complete way of life. The Arabic word islam itself means ‘submission’ or ‘surrender’. For Muslims, every action — eating, working, praying, giving — is an act of worship when carried out with the right intention (niyyah). This holistic understanding means that the rituals Muslims perform are not separate from daily life but are woven into it.

The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Sunni Muslims structure their faith around the Five Pillars. The analogy of a house and its pillars is often used: just as a house collapses without structural supports, a Muslim’s faith would collapse without these five foundations.

  • Shahadah — the declaration of faith
  • Salat — five daily prayers
  • Zakat — compulsory almsgiving (2.5% of savings)
  • Sawm — fasting during Ramadan
  • Hajj — pilgrimage to Mecca at least once in a lifetime
Key Fact

The Five Pillars are obligatory for every Sunni Muslim who is able to fulfil them. Together they represent the structural framework of Muslim life, combining declaration, prayer, charity, self-discipline and pilgrimage.

The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims organise their practice around the Ten Obligatory Acts (known in Arabic as the ‘Furu’ ad-Din’, or branches of the faith). These go beyond the Five Pillars and include additional duties specific to Shi’a practice:

  1. Salat — five daily prayers
  2. Sawm — fasting
  3. Zakat — charitable giving
  4. Khums — a twenty percent tax on certain earnings, paid to the Imam or his representatives
  5. Hajj — pilgrimage to Mecca
  6. Jihad — striving in the way of Allah (see below)
  7. Amr-bil-Maroof — commanding what is right
  8. Nahi Anil Munkar — forbidding what is wrong
  9. Tawalla — expressing love for the friends of Allah (the Imams and their followers)
  10. Tabarra — expressing disassociation from the enemies of Allah

Both traditions share the same core practices — prayer, fasting, almsgiving and pilgrimage. The Shi’a Ten Obligatory Acts extend this framework to include Khums (a second form of financial giving), Jihad as a religious duty, and the paired obligations of Amr-bil-Maroof and Nahi Anil Munkar (promoting good and forbidding evil). Tawalla and Tabarra reflect Shi’a loyalty to the Imams and theological boundaries. A common misconception is that the Shi’a reject the Five Pillars — in fact they perform the same core acts but within a broader obligatory framework. Examiners often ask students to compare these two structures, so knowing all ten acts by name is essential.

The Shahadah

The Shahadah is the declaration: la ilaha illa-llah, muhammadur-rasulu-llah — “There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.” It is unique among the Five Pillars because it is the only one that is not an action. Saying the Shahadah with sincerity is itself an act of worship.

The Shahadah punctuates the key moments of a Muslim’s life. It is whispered as the first words into the ear of a newborn baby. It is recited at the moment of conversion to Islam. It is said at, or to, a person who is dying. Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is the theological heart of the Shahadah: there is no partner, equal or associate to Allah.

Key Fact

The Shahadah — la ilaha illa-llah, muhammadur-rasulu-llah — is said at birth, conversion and death. It is the only ‘non-action’ pillar: speaking it sincerely is itself an act of submission to Allah, confirming belief in Tawhid.

Salah: Five Daily Prayers

Salah is direct communication with Allah. The Qur’an instructs: “Maintain with care the [obligatory] prayers and [in particular] the middle prayer and stand before Allah, devoutly obedient” (Surah 2:238, al-Baqarah). Muslims pray five times a day: Fajr (before dawn), Zuhr (midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (after sunset) and Isha (night).

Before prayer, Muslims must perform wudu (ritual ablution). The worshipper washes the face, hands and arms to the elbow, wipes the head and washes the feet. This physical purification represents spiritual readiness to stand before Allah. The direction of prayer — facing Mecca — is called the qibla. Each unit of prayer is called a raka’t. Different prayers have different numbers of raka’t.

Jummah is the Friday midday prayer, which replaces Zuhr and is obligatory for adult Muslim men. The Qur’an says: “O you who have believed, when [the adhan] is called for the prayer on the day of Jumu’ah [Friday], then proceed to the remembrance of Allah” (Surah 62:9, al-Jumuah). The prayer is preceded by the khutba — a sermon given by the imam covering both religious and community matters. Women are permitted but not required to attend Jummah. In Muslim-majority countries, businesses often close at midday on Fridays to allow attendance.

Du’a: Personal Supplication

Du’a is private, personal prayer. Unlike Salah, which follows a fixed set of Arabic recitations in specific body positions at set times, du’a can be spoken in any language, at any time and in any posture. It is the Muslim speaking directly and intimately to Allah from the heart. The Qur’an promises: “And when My servants ask you concerning Me — indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me” (Surah 2:186, al-Baqarah). Du’a is used to express gratitude, seek forgiveness, ask for guidance and pray for others. It reflects the deeply personal dimension of a Muslim’s relationship with Allah, beyond the structure of formal worship.

How Do Believers Think God Is Revealed?

Many religious believers do not arrive at their faith primarily through philosophical arguments. Instead, they claim direct or indirect experience of God. The idea that God makes himself known to human beings is called revelation. Christian theology traditionally distinguishes two kinds: general revelation (available to everyone, through creation and conscience) and special revelation (specific acts of God, such as scripture or the incarnation of Jesus Christ).

The opening of John’s Gospel (John 1:14) expresses the Christian conviction that God’s ultimate act of self-revelation was becoming human: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.” This is the doctrine of the incarnation — that Jesus Christ is the Word of God made visible in human form. For Christians, knowing Jesus is the most direct way of knowing God.

Other means through which believers say God is revealed include: meeting inspirational people whose lives seem to embody divine goodness; encountering scripture; the voice of conscience; and God’s apparent action in history. In Islam, revelation came through the angel Jibril to the Prophet Muhammad, producing the Qur’an as the final and perfect word of Allah. Jewish believers point to the Torah as the revealed law given to Moses at Sinai.

Key Fact

Revelation takes many forms: through scripture (the Bible, Qur’an, Torah), through the person of Jesus Christ (“The Word became flesh” — John 1:14), through conscience, through creation, through miracles, and through personal religious experience. Together these constitute the “sources of wisdom and authority” that believers draw on.

Miracles

Miracles are events that seem to go beyond what natural causes can produce, and which believers attribute to divine action. The Gospels record many miracles attributed to Jesus: healing the sick, walking on water, feeding five thousand people, and most significantly, the resurrection. For Christians, miracles are signs that God is active in the world and that the natural order is not closed to divine intervention.

The philosopher David Hume argued that belief in miracles is almost never justified. He defined a miracle as a violation of a law of nature, and argued that the evidence in favour of the natural law will always be stronger than the testimony of those who claim to have witnessed a miracle. People are prone to exaggeration and superstition. However, believers respond that Hume’s argument presupposes naturalism — the view that only natural causes exist — and so begs the very question at issue. If God exists, miracles are entirely possible.

Believers argue that miracles, especially the resurrection of Jesus, are strong evidence for God’s existence and power. If the resurrection happened, it demonstrates a God who can act in history and who validated Jesus’s claims. Many point to unexplained healings at places of pilgrimage such as Lourdes as continuing evidence of miraculous divine action.

Non-believers argue that what appear to be miracles are more likely to be coincidences, natural events not yet understood by science, or wishful thinking by people in emotionally heightened states. Humanists reject miracles entirely — they see the natural universe as self-contained and believe that religious reports of miracles reflect deeply held cultural and psychological needs rather than actual supernatural events. For the 15-mark “Discuss” format, presenting both views fairly and then evaluating which is more compelling is essential.

Forms of Religious Experience

Many people claim to have had direct experience of God or the divine. Philosophers and theologians have identified several types of religious experience.

Conversion involves a dramatic change of belief or life direction in response to what the person perceives as a divine encounter. The most famous example in the Christian tradition is the conversion of Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–6). Saul was a persecutor of early Christians when he reported being struck down by a blinding light and hearing the voice of Jesus. He was left blind for three days and emerged as Paul, one of the most influential figures in early Christianity. His conversion was sudden, unexpected and transformative — the hallmarks many see as confirming its divine origin.

Key Fact

Saul’s conversion (Acts 9:1–6) is the specification’s named example of a conversion experience. He heard the voice of Jesus saying, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” Examiners may ask you to describe this event and evaluate whether it constitutes evidence for God’s existence.

Mystical experience is a profound sense of union with God or ultimate reality. It is typically described as indescribable, overwhelming, and accompanied by deep peace or insight. The philosopher William James identified four features common to mystical experiences: they are noetic (they convey knowledge), they are transient (short-lived), they are passive (the person feels acted upon, not acting), and they are ineffable (impossible to fully put into words). Many Christian mystics — such as Teresa of Avila and Julian of Norwich — described such experiences.

Charismatic and ecstatic experience is associated with the gifts of the Holy Spirit described in the New Testament. In charismatic worship, believers may speak in tongues (glossolalia), prophesy, or experience intense emotion as they feel the Holy Spirit moving among them. This form of experience is common in Pentecostal churches and Charismatic Catholic movements.

Visions and the Sacraments

Visions are supernatural perceptions in which a person claims to see or hear God, Jesus, Mary or another spiritual figure. They may be experienced with the physical eyes or as vivid images in the mind. Biblical examples include Isaiah’s vision of God’s throne (Isaiah 6) and John’s Revelation. In the modern era, many Catholics report appearances of the Virgin Mary at sites such as Fatima and Lourdes.

For many Christians, God is also encountered through worship and the sacraments. The Mass or Holy Communion is considered by Catholics and many other Christians to be a moment of genuine encounter with the risen Christ. During the Eucharist, the ordinary — bread and wine — becomes a vehicle for the extraordinary: the presence of God. This sacramental understanding means that for millions of believers, religious experience is not reserved for dramatic visions or conversions; it is available in the regular acts of corporate worship.

Believers argue that the widespread, cross-cultural nature of religious experience — reported across all traditions, in all times and places — is strong evidence that it points to a genuine spiritual reality. They apply the “principle of credulity” (Richard Swinburne): if an experience seems real, we should take it at face value unless there is specific reason not to. The sheer number and consistency of reports makes it implausible that all are wishful thinking or delusion.

Non-believers argue that religious experiences can be explained psychologically (wish-fulfilment, grief, suggestion) or neurologically (temporal lobe activity, oxygen deprivation). Sigmund Freud argued that belief in God is a form of collective wish-fulfilment — humanity’s desire for a cosmic parent figure. The fact that people’s religious experiences are shaped by their own culture (a Christian sees Jesus; a Muslim encounters Allah; a Buddhist experiences nibbana) suggests the experiences reflect prior belief rather than objective reality.
